iberia.description: Alfonso XIII’s Spain, shaken by the loss of Cuba (1898) and the Barcelona Tragic Week (1909), stays neutral in 1914. Portugal has been a republic since October 1910 and will enter the war in 1916. Genetics: continuity with emigration.

britain.description: Asquith’s Liberal government has curbed the Lords (1911) and passed Irish Home Rule, while Ulster unionists and Irish nationalists arm. Britain enters the war on 4 August 1914 after Germany invades Belgium. Genetics: continuity.

france.description: Poincaré’s France is allied with Russia and draws closer to Britain. Paris is the art capital of the world (Cubism, the Ballets Russes, Proust). Jaurès is assassinated on 31 July; Germany declares war on 3 August and the Marne halts the invasion in September. Genetics: continuity.

central.description: Germany, Europe’s strongest industrial economy, backs Austria-Hungary with the ‘blank cheque’ of 5 July 1914. Vienna, Budapest and Prague are capitals of modernism. Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia on 28 July. Genetics: continuity.

scandinavia.description: Norway has been independent since 1905; Sweden and Denmark declare neutrality in August 1914. Finland is a Russian grand duchy with its own parliament (elected by universal suffrage since 1906) under renewed Russification. Genetics: continuity.

italy.description: Italy, a member of the Triple Alliance, declares neutrality in August 1914 and will join the Entente in 1915 for Trentino and Trieste. The Libyan war (1911–12) and Futurism mark a restless young state. Genetics: continuity.

balkans.description: The Balkan Wars of 1912–13 divide Ottoman Macedonia and Thrace among Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria, and create Albania. Austria-Hungary, which annexed Bosnia in 1908, sees an enlarged Serbia as a deadly threat. Genetics: continuity with forced migration.

eastern.description: Nicholas II’s empire is industrialising fast, governed with a weak Duma after 1905. It mobilises in support of Serbia on 30 July 1914. The Ottoman Empire, run by the Committee of Union and Progress, signs a secret alliance with Germany on 2 August. Genetics: continuity.

GBR.art: Vorticism; the Post-Impressionist exhibitions (1910, 1912). Roger Fry’s Omega Workshops (1913); Wyndham Lewis’s Blast (1914).
GBR.ideas: New Liberalism: pensions (1908), national insurance (1911), the Parliament Act (1911). The Labour Party, founded 1900, holds 42 seats after December 1910.
GBR.literature: Conrad, Hardy, Shaw, E. M. Forster’s Howards End (1910); D. H. Lawrence’s Sons and Lovers (1913). H. G. Wells and Arnold Bennett write of the new lower-middle class; Rupert Brooke’s war sonnets follow in 1914.
GBR.philosophy: Russell and Whitehead’s Principia Mathematica (1910–13). G. E. Moore’s Principia Ethica (1903) shapes the Bloomsbury group.
GBR.science: Rutherford’s nuclear model (1911); Moseley’s atomic numbers (1913).
GBR.story: On 3 August 1914 Grey tells the Commons why Britain cannot stand aside if Belgium is invaded; the ultimatum to Germany expires at 11 p.m. London time on 4 August. On the 5th the British Expeditionary Force begins crossing to France; it fights at Mons on 23 August.

IRL.art: Celtic Revival design; Jack B. Yeats. Harry Clarke begins his stained glass; the Hugh Lane Gallery controversy (1913).
IRL.ideas: Home Rule versus unionism; republican separatism. Arthur Griffith’s Sinn Féin and the Irish Republican Brotherhood argue for full separation. Larkin and James Connolly’s Irish Citizen Army (1913) gives labour its own militia.

images.alt: W. B. Yeats — George Charles Beresford, 1911
images.caption: W. B. Yeats — George Charles Beresford, 1911

IRL.literature: Yeats, Synge’s The Playboy of the Western World (1907), Joyce’s Dubliners (1914). Lady Gregory and Yeats run the Abbey; Joyce’s Dubliners is published in June 1914.
IRL.philosophy: Cultural nationalism. Patrick Pearse writes on education and blood sacrifice.
IRL.science: Harland & Wolff, Belfast, builders of the Titanic (1912). Belfast is an industrial city of shipyards, ropeworks and linen mills.
IRL.story: In September 1914 Home Rule becomes law and is suspended in the same breath; Redmond urges the Volunteers to fight for Britain, splitting the movement that will rise at Easter 1916. In the Curragh incident of March 1914 British officers say they will resign rather than coerce Ulster; in April unionists land 25,000 rifles at Larne, and in July the Irish Volunteers land their own at Howth.

FRA.art: Picasso and Braque’s cubism; Matisse; Delaunay. The Salon d’Automne and the Section d’Or; Robert and Sonia Delaunay’s Orphism.
FRA.ideas: Laïcité, revanche for Alsace-Lorraine, syndicalism. The 1913 Three-Year Law extends military service to three years.
FRA.literature: Proust’s Swann’s Way (1913); Apollinaire’s Alcools (1913); Alain-Fournier’s Le Grand Meaulnes (1913). Charles Péguy, killed at the Marne in September 1914.
FRA.philosophy: Henri Bergson’s Creative Evolution (1907); Durkheim. Bergson’s lectures at the Collège de France attract crowds.
FRA.science: Marie Curie’s second Nobel Prize (1911); Poincaré’s mathematics. Henri Poincaré (d. 1912); Louis Blériot crosses the Channel by air on 25 July 1909.
FRA.story: On 29 May 1913 Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring, danced by the Ballets Russes in Nijinsky’s choreography, provokes uproar at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées. Jaurès, the socialist leader who has campaigned against war, is shot in a Paris café on 31 July; on 4 August his opponents and supporters together vote war credits in the ‘Sacred Union’.

ESP.art: Gaudí’s Sagrada Família; Picasso’s Barcelona beginnings. Picasso and Juan Gris in Paris; Joaquín Sorolla’s light-filled seascapes. Gaudí’s Casa Milà (1906–12).
ESP.ideas: Regenerationism. Joaquín Costa’s ‘school and larder’ regenerationism.
ESP.literature: Unamuno’s Niebla (1914); Antonio Machado’s Campos de Castilla (1912). Valle-Inclán, Pío Baroja and Azorín of the Generation of ’98.
ESP.philosophy: José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditaciones del Quijote (1914).
ESP.science: Santiago Ramón y Cajal, Nobel Prize 1906. Ramón y Cajal’s neuron doctrine shows that the nervous system is made of separate cells; he shares the 1906 Nobel Prize with Golgi.
ESP.story: When the army calls up Catalan reservists for Morocco in July 1909, Barcelona rises; churches burn in the Tragic Week and the anarchist educator Ferrer is executed. When war breaks out, Spain declares neutrality and its factories and mines profit from Allied orders.

PRT.art: Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso’s modernism. Souza-Cardoso shows at the Armory Show in New York (1913). Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro’s portraits.
PRT.ideas: Republican secularism. Anticlericalism and positivism; the 1911 Constitution.

images.alt: Act of proclamation of the Portuguese Republic, 1910
images.caption: Act of proclamation of the Portuguese Republic, 1910

images.alt: Manuel II, the last king — Joshua Benoliel
images.caption: Manuel II, the last king — Joshua Benoliel

PRT.literature: Fernando Pessoa and Mário de Sá-Carneiro prepare Orpheu (1915). Pessoa, who has returned from Durban in 1905, invents his heteronyms Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis and Álvaro de Campos in 1914.
PRT.philosophy: Republican positivism (Teófilo Braga). Teófilo Braga, philosopher and literary historian, provisional president (1910–11) and president (1915).
PRT.science: Egas Moniz’s early career in Lisbon. The University of Lisbon and the University of Porto are founded in 1911.
PRT.story: The revolution of October 1910 sends King Manuel II into exile in England and ends almost eight centuries of monarchy. The revolution begins on 3–4 October 1910 with mutinies in the navy and army; the republic is proclaimed from the balcony of Lisbon’s city hall on 5 October.

NLD.art: Mondrian in Paris (1912–14); Berlage. Mondrian, in Paris from 1912, moves from trees to abstract grids; Jan Toorop’s symbolist works. Kees van Dongen in Paris.
NLD.ideas: Neutrality and international law. The ‘schools struggle’ over state funding of religious schools, settled in 1917.
NLD.literature: Louis Couperus; Herman Gorter. Couperus’s Old People and the Things that Pass (1906).
NLD.philosophy: Gerard Heymans’s psychology. Heymans in Groningen; Hugo de Vries’s mutation theory.
NLD.science: Kamerlingh Onnes discovers superconductivity (1911; Nobel 1913); Lorentz. Lorentz (Nobel 1902) supplies the transformations used in relativity; Kamerlingh Onnes liquefies helium (1908).
NLD.story: The Peace Palace in The Hague, funded by Andrew Carnegie, opens on 28 August 1913, home of the Permanent Court of Arbitration—a year before the war. The Peace Palace houses the Permanent Court of Arbitration set up at the Hague Peace Conference of 1899; the second conference was held in 1907, and a third was planned for 1915.

BEL.art: Victor Horta; James Ensor. Horta’s Hôtel Tassel (1893) is the first Art Nouveau house; Ensor’s masks; Fernand Khnopff.
BEL.ideas: Guaranteed neutrality (Treaty of London, 1839). Universal male suffrage with plural votes (1893); the Congo taken over from Leopold II (1908).

images.alt: Ruins of the university library, Leuven, 1914
images.caption: Ruins of the university library, Leuven, 1914

BEL.literature: Maurice Maeterlinck, Nobel Prize 1911; Verhaeren. Émile Verhaeren’s poems of the industrial city; Maeterlinck’s The Blue Bird (1908). Georges Eekhoud and Stijn Streuvels (in Flemish).
BEL.philosophy: Cardinal Mercier’s neo-Thomism at Leuven. Paul Otlet and Henri La Fontaine’s Mundaneum and Universal Decimal Classification.
BEL.science: Solvay conferences (1911). Ernest Solvay funds the first Solvay physics conference in Brussels (1911), with Einstein, Planck and Curie.
BEL.story: On 2 August Germany demands passage; Albert refuses. Leuven’s university library burns on 25–26 August, becoming a symbol of the war on civilians. German troops shoot hundreds of civilians in Dinant, Andenne and Leuven during the advance; the burning of the university library and its manuscripts turns world opinion against Germany.

DEU.art: Die Brücke (Dresden, 1905); Der Blaue Reiter (Munich, 1911). Peter Behrens designs AEG factories and products; Walter Gropius’s Fagus Works (1911–13); the Werkbund exhibition in Cologne (1914).
DEU.ideas: Weltpolitik; Social Democracy; nationalism. Pan-German League and Navy League agitation.
DEU.literature: Thomas Mann’s Death in Venice (1912); Rilke; Stefan George. Gerhart Hauptmann (Nobel 1912); Heinrich Mann.
DEU.philosophy: Max Weber; Husserl’s phenomenology. Neo-Kantianism at Marburg (Hermann Cohen) and the Heidelberg sociologists.
DEU.science: Max Planck; Einstein moves to Berlin in 1914; Haber–Bosch ammonia. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch make ammonia from air (1909–13); Wilhelm Röntgen’s X-rays (1895).
DEU.story: On 5 July 1914 Wilhelm II and Bethmann Hollweg promise Austria-Hungary German backing against Serbia—the ‘blank cheque’ that turns a Balkan crisis into a European war. Moltke’s plan sends seven armies through Belgium and Luxembourg to envelop France in six weeks, leaving one to hold East Prussia; the Russian invasion of East Prussia is destroyed at Tannenberg (26–30 August).

AUT.art: Klimt’s golden period; Schiele; Adolf Loos; Schoenberg’s atonality. Otto Wagner’s Postal Savings Bank (1906); the Wiener Werkstätte; Kokoschka’s The Bride of the Wind (1913–14).
AUT.ideas: Dynastic patriotism versus nationalism. Austro-Marxists Karl Renner and Otto Bauer propose cultural autonomy for nationalities.

images.alt: Freud and colleagues at Clark University, 1909
images.caption: Freud and colleagues at Clark University, 1909

AUT.literature: Karl Kraus’s Die Fackel; Schnitzler; Hofmannsthal. Stefan Zweig; Robert Musil’s Young Törless (1906); Georg Trakl, who dies in Kraków in November 1914.
AUT.philosophy: Freud’s psychoanalysis; Wittgenstein’s early logic. Ernst Mach’s empiricism; Ludwig von Mises and the Austrian school of economics.
AUT.science: Mach; Boltzmann; Lise Meitner (Vienna-trained). Karl Landsteiner discovers blood groups (1901); Victor Hess discovers cosmic rays in balloon flights (1912).
AUT.story: Vienna sends Serbia an ultimatum on 23 July 1914 designed to be rejected, and declares war on 28 July. Conrad von Hötzendorf has urged war on Serbia again and again since 1906; after Sarajevo the old emperor agrees, with Germany’s promise of support.

HUN.art: Hungarian Secession; Budapest Parliament (1904). Ödön Lechner’s Hungarian Art Nouveau (Museum of Applied Arts); the painters of Nagybánya. Bartók’s Bluebeard’s Castle (1911).
HUN.ideas: Magyarisation; dualism. Liberal nationalism that limits the vote to protect Magyar dominance.
HUN.literature: Endre Ady; the journal Nyugat (1908). Ady’s New Poems (1906) shocks with its symbolism; Mihály Babits and Dezső Kosztolányi write for Nyugat.
HUN.philosophy: Lukács’s early work. Georg Lukács and Karl Mannheim in the Sunday Circle.
HUN.science: Eötvös’s torsion balance. Loránd Eötvös’s torsion balance measures gravity with precision.
HUN.story: Tisza at first opposes war with Serbia, fearing more Slavs in the monarchy; by 14 July he gives way. Tisza, who has crushed parliamentary obstruction by force in 1912, is the strongest politician in the monarchy; his consent decides that the ultimatum will be sent.

CZE.art: Mucha; the Municipal House (1912); Janáček’s Jenůfa (1904). Czech cubist architecture (Josef Gočár’s House of the Black Madonna, 1912); Kupka in Paris.
CZE.ideas: Czech state right and Austro-Slavism. Masaryk’s ‘realism’: Czech national rights through democracy and truth in history. Social Democrats split along national lines (1911).

images.alt: Mucha at work on the Slav Epic
images.caption: Mucha at work on the Slav Epic

CZE.literature: Franz Kafka (The Judgment, 1912); Jaroslav Hašek. Otokar Březina’s symbolist verse; Rilke and Werfel, Prague-born German poets.
CZE.philosophy: Masaryk. Masaryk, professor in Prague, exposed the forged ‘medieval’ manuscripts in the 1880s.
CZE.science: Škoda Works, Plzeň, the monarchy’s arsenal. Škoda builds the monarchy’s heavy guns, including the 30.5 cm mortar.
CZE.story: In December 1914 Masaryk leaves Austria and begins the campaign abroad for an independent Czechoslovakia. Kafka, a German-speaking Jewish insurance official, writes The Trial in Prague in the autumn of 1914; Hašek, who will create the good soldier Švejk, is a bohemian journalist.

BIH.art: Habsburg pseudo-Moorish architecture. Habsburg architects build Sarajevo’s city hall (Vijećnica) in a pseudo-Moorish style.
BIH.ideas: South Slav (Yugoslav) nationalism. Young Bosnia’s students read anarchist and nationalist writers. Habsburg administrator Benjamin Kállay (1882–1903) promoted a ‘Bosnian’ identity to counter Serb and Croat nationalism.
BIH.literature: Young Bosnia’s poets; later Ivo Andrić. Petar Kočić’s stories of Bosnian peasants.
BIH.philosophy: Young Bosnia’s revolutionary nationalism. Revolutionary nationalism among high-school students.
BIH.science: Habsburg railways and mines. The Habsburgs build narrow-gauge railways, mines and forestry works.
BIH.story: On 28 June 1914 the archduke’s car takes a wrong turn near the Latin Bridge; Gavrilo Princip shoots Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie. Princip is one of six assassins armed in Belgrade with the help of officers of the Black Hand; Čabrinović’s bomb misses, but the archduke’s driver later turns into Franz Joseph Street and stops.

POL.art: Wyspiański; Malczewski. Jacek Malczewski’s symbolism; the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts. Józef Mehoffer’s stained glass for Fribourg Cathedral.
POL.ideas: Independence versus cooperation. Piłsudski’s armed struggle against Russia versus Dmowski’s national democracy.
POL.literature: Henryk Sienkiewicz, Nobel Prize 1905; Reymont’s The Peasants (1904–09). Stefan Żeromski’s novels; Wyspiański’s The Wedding (1901).
POL.philosophy: Positivism and Young Poland modernism; Kazimierz Twardowski’s Lwów school of logic.
POL.science: Marie Skłodowska-Curie. Skłodowska-Curie, born in Warsaw, wins Nobel Prizes in physics (1903) and chemistry (1911).
POL.story: On 6 August 1914 Piłsudski’s First Cadre Company crosses from Austrian Galicia into Russian Poland. Piłsudski hopes to raise Russian Poland against the tsar; his riflemen get a cool welcome in Kielce. His Legions fight for Austria, while Dmowski’s National Democrats back Russia.

RUS.art: Kandinsky, Goncharova, Malevich; Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring. Malevich’s first Suprematist works follow in 1915; Natalia Goncharova and Mikhail Larionov’s Rayonism.
RUS.ideas: Autocracy versus liberalism and revolution. Lenin’s Bolsheviks and the Mensheviks split the Social Democrats (1903); the Kadets lead the liberals.

images.alt: Chamber of the State Duma, Tauride Palace
images.caption: Chamber of the State Duma, Tauride Palace

RUS.literature: Blok, Akhmatova, Bely’s Petersburg (1913–14). Maxim Gorky; Anna Akhmatova’s Evening (1912) and Rosary (1914); the Futurists’ A Slap in the Face of Public Taste (1912).
RUS.philosophy: Berdyaev; Russian religious philosophy. The Vekhi (Landmarks) symposium of 1909 attacks the radical intelligentsia.
RUS.science: Pavlov, Nobel Prize 1904. Pavlov’s conditioned reflexes; Konstantin Tsiolkovsky’s rocket equation (1903); Igor Sikorsky’s four-engined Ilya Muromets airliner (1913).
RUS.story: St Petersburg is renamed Petrograd in August 1914 to sound less German. Sazonov persuades the tsar to order general mobilisation on 30 July; Germany demands it be stopped and declares war on 1 August. Crowds kneel before the Winter Palace as Nicholas II swears not to make peace while an enemy remains on Russian soil.

FIN.art: Sibelius; Gallen-Kallela. Eliel Saarinen designs Helsinki railway station (competition 1904); Gallen-Kallela’s Kalevala paintings. Akseli Gallen-Kallela’s Kalevala frescoes in the National Museum.
FIN.ideas: Constitutional nationalism. Legalists, ‘compliants’ and activists differ on resisting Russification. Activist students start secret contacts with Germany late in 1914 (the Jäger movement).

images.alt: The first women members of parliament, Finland, 1907
images.caption: The first women members of parliament, Finland, 1907

FIN.literature: Eino Leino’s poetry. Leino’s Whitsongs (1903); Juhani Aho. Maria Jotuni and the new women writers.
FIN.philosophy: Snellman’s legacy. Edvard Westermarck’s sociology of morals.
FIN.science: Helsinki University and Finnish engineering. The Helsinki University of Technology (1908).
FIN.story: The 1906 Parliament Act replaces the four-estate Diet with a single chamber of 200 members elected by all adults. In the March 1907 election 19 women are elected, the first women members of a national parliament anywhere; nine of them are Social Democrats.

UKR.art: Oleksandr Murashko; Kyiv modernism. Mykola Lysenko’s operas; Lviv’s Grand Theatre (1900). Heorhiy Narbut’s graphic art.
UKR.ideas: Ukrainian national movement. Federalism within Russia, autonomy within Austria, or independence. The Union for the Liberation of Ukraine, founded in Lviv in August 1914, hopes for a Central Powers victory.

images.alt: Taras Shevchenko, whose 1914 centenary was banned (Kramskoi, 1871)
images.caption: Taras Shevchenko, whose 1914 centenary was banned (Kramskoi, 1871)

UKR.literature: Ivan Franko; Lesya Ukrainka (d. 1913). Franko’s Moses (1905); Mykhailo Kotsiubynsky’s Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors (1911). Volodymyr Vynnychenko’s plays and novels.
UKR.philosophy: Hrushevsky’s History of Ukraine-Rus’. Hrushevsky’s ten-volume History of Ukraine-Rus’ (from 1898) gives Ukraine its own national history.
UKR.science: Shevchenko Scientific Society (Lviv). The Shevchenko Scientific Society in Lviv acts as a Ukrainian academy of sciences.
UKR.story: In January 1914 the Russian Minister of the Interior bans public commemoration of the centenary of Taras Shevchenko’s birth; students in Kyiv demonstrate anyway and are dispersed by police.

SWE.art: Carl Larsson’s domestic idylls; Anders Zorn. Larsson’s watercolours of his family home at Sundborn; Ragnar Östberg’s City Hall (begun 1911).
SWE.ideas: Parliamentarism versus royal power; universal male suffrage (1909). The Social Democrats, led by Hjalmar Branting, become the largest party in the Second Chamber in 1914.

images.alt: Carl Larsson, Breakfast under the Big Birch (1896)
images.caption: Carl Larsson, Breakfast under the Big Birch (1896)

SWE.literature: Selma Lagerlöf, first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1909); August Strindberg. Hjalmar Söderberg; Verner von Heidenstam (Nobel 1916). Pär Lagerkvist’s expressionist Word Art and Picture Art (1913).
SWE.philosophy: Ellen Key’s writings on childhood and women’s rights. Axel Hägerström’s Uppsala school.
SWE.science: The Nobel Prizes, awarded in Stockholm since 1901; Svante Arrhenius. Arrhenius (Nobel 1903) explains how carbon dioxide warms the climate (1896); Gustaf Dalén (Nobel 1912) for lighthouse technology.
SWE.story: On 6 February 1914 some 30,000 farmers march to Stockholm Palace; in the Courtyard Speech Gustaf V promises them stronger defences, against his Liberal government. Karl Staaff resigns and a non-party ministry under Hjalmar Hammarskjöld takes over. Sweden declares neutrality in August 1914 and, with Norway and Denmark, the three kings meet at Malmö in December to affirm it.

NOR.art: Edvard Munch, whose murals for the University of Oslo’s Aula are installed in 1916. Munch wins the competition for the University Aula, painting The Sun (1911). Gustav Vigeland works on the great fountain commissioned by Kristiania in 1906.
NOR.ideas: Women gain the vote in national elections in 1913. Norway gives women the national vote in 1913, after Finland (1906).

images.alt: Scott’s party at Amundsen’s tent at the South Pole, January 1912
images.caption: Scott’s party at Amundsen’s tent at the South Pole, January 1912

images.alt: Munch, The Sun (1911), for the University Aula
images.caption: Munch, The Sun (1911), for the University Aula

NOR.literature: Knut Hamsun; Sigrid Undset’s early novels. Hamsun’s Hunger (1890) and Growth of the Soil (1917); Undset’s Jenny (1911). Olav Duun and Johan Bojer; Henrik Ibsen (d. 1906).
NOR.philosophy: Language politics as national identity. Ivar Aasen’s Landsmål as a nation’s own written language. Nansen’s humanitarian internationalism.
NOR.science: Polar exploration: Nansen and Amundsen; Kristian Birkeland’s aurora research. Birkeland’s aurora expeditions; Fridtjof Nansen’s oceanography.
NOR.story: Roald Amundsen reaches the South Pole on 14 December 1911. Amundsen’s party of five, with sledge dogs, beats Robert Falcon Scott’s British expedition by five weeks; Scott finds Amundsen’s tent at the pole in January 1912 and dies on the return.

DNK.art: Vilhelm Hammershøi’s quiet interiors; Carl Nielsen’s symphonies. Hammershøi’s grey rooms in Strandgade. Carl Nielsen’s Fourth Symphony (‘The Inextinguishable’) begun in 1914.
DNK.ideas: Neutrality and a new democratic constitution (1915), giving women the vote. Cooperative movement among farmers. The Radicals’ government of 1913 prepares women’s suffrage.
DNK.literature: Henrik Pontoppidan (Nobel Prize 1917); Johannes V. Jensen. Pontoppidan’s Lucky Per (1898–1904); Karen Blixen leaves for Kenya in 1913. Martin Andersen Nexø’s Pelle the Conqueror (1906–10).
DNK.philosophy: Harald Høffding; Kierkegaard’s growing reputation. Høffding’s philosophy of religion.
DNK.science: Niels Bohr’s atom (1913). Bohr (Nobel 1922); the Carlsberg Laboratory.
DNK.story: In 1913 Niels Bohr, back in Copenhagen from Rutherford’s Manchester laboratory, publishes his model of the atom with electrons in fixed orbits. Bohr’s three-part paper of 1913 combines Rutherford’s nuclear atom with Planck’s quantum, explaining the spectral lines of hydrogen. Christian X declares neutrality in August 1914.

CHE.art: Ferdinand Hodler. Hodler’s The Woodcutter (1910) and his history paintings.
CHE.ideas: Direct democracy and neutrality. The 1874 constitution introduced referendums; the popular initiative followed in 1891. Neutrality guaranteed by the great powers in 1815.
CHE.literature: Carl Spitteler’s ‘Our Swiss Standpoint’ speech (December 1914) calls for neutrality of the heart. Spitteler, Nobel 1919. Robert Walser’s Jakob von Gunten (1909); Charles-Ferdinand Ramuz.
CHE.philosophy: Ferdinand de Saussure (d. 1913); Carl Jung breaks with Freud (1913). Saussure’s course in general linguistics, published by his students in 1916.
CHE.science: ETH Zurich; Einstein’s Bern years. Einstein’s Bern years produce special relativity and the light-quantum (1905).
CHE.story: Einstein publishes special relativity in 1905 while at the Bern patent office. Einstein becomes a professor in Zurich and Prague and returns to Zurich’s ETH in 1912 before leaving for Berlin in 1914. Switzerland becomes the home of the International Committee of the Red Cross’s prisoner-of-war agency (opened in Geneva in August 1914).

ITA.art: Umberto Boccioni and Giacomo Balla’s Futurist painting. Boccioni’s Unique Forms of Continuity in Space (1913).
ITA.ideas: Irredentism: Trentino and Trieste still Austrian. Italian nationalism (Enrico Corradini’s Nationalist Association, 1910).

images.alt: Boccioni, Unique Forms of Continuity in Space (1913)
images.caption: Boccioni, Unique Forms of Continuity in Space (1913)

ITA.literature: Gabriele D’Annunzio; Luigi Pirandello; Grazia Deledda. Pirandello’s The Late Mattia Pascal (1904).
ITA.philosophy: Benedetto Croce’s idealism; Giovanni Gentile. Croce’s journal La Critica. Vilfredo Pareto’s theory of elites.
ITA.science: Marconi, Nobel Prize 1909; Montessori. Marconi’s wireless telegraphy; Maria Montessori’s method of teaching (1907).
ITA.story: Marinetti’s Futurist Manifesto appears on the front page of Le Figaro on 20 February 1909, praising speed, machines and war as ‘the world’s only hygiene’. The Futurists hold violent ‘serate’ evenings in theatres and campaign for war in 1914–15. Italy refuses to follow its allies in August 1914, because Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia without consulting it; Salandra’s ‘sacred egoism’ bargains with both sides.

SRB.art: Nadežda Petrović’s expressionism. Petrović paints expressionist landscapes and works as a nurse in the Balkan Wars.
SRB.ideas: Yugoslav unity; the secret ‘Black Hand’ in the officer corps. Yugoslavism among Croat and Slovene students.

images.alt: King Peter watching the Battle of Cer, August 1914
images.caption: King Peter watching the Battle of Cer, August 1914

SRB.literature: Jovan Skerlić; Branislav Nušić’s comedies. Jovan Dučić and Milan Rakić’s verse; Skerlić’s history of Serbian literature. Borisav Stanković’s Impure Blood (1910).
SRB.philosophy: Liberal and radical political thought around Pašić. Liberal-radical constitutionalism after 1903.
SRB.science: Mihajlo Pupin and Nikola Tesla abroad; Mihailo Petrović Alas in Belgrade. Belgrade University (1905); Mihailo Petrović Alas’s mathematics.
SRB.story: At Cer in August 1914 the Serbian army defeats the Austro-Hungarian invasion. General Stepa Stepanović’s Second Army defeats Potiorek’s forces at Cer mountain in mid-August, the first Allied victory of the war.

GRC.art: Neoclassical Athens of Ziller and the Hansens. The National Archaeological Museum and the Athens Academy. Nikolaos Gyzis (d. 1901) and the Munich school.
GRC.ideas: The Megali Idea of uniting all Greeks. Venizelism versus royalism. Venizelos favours the Entente; Constantine, the Kaiser’s brother-in-law, favours neutrality.

images.alt: The Greek army enters Thessaloniki, 1912 — Achille Beltrame
images.caption: The Greek army enters Thessaloniki, 1912 — Achille Beltrame

GRC.literature: Constantine Cavafy in Alexandria; Kostis Palamas. Palamas’s The Twelve Lays of the Gypsy (1907); Cavafy’s Ithaka (1911). Angelos Sikelianos’s The Visionary (1909).
GRC.philosophy: The ‘language question’: demotic Greek against katharevousa. The demotic-versus-katharevousa language question.
GRC.science: The National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.
GRC.story: Under the 1913 Treaty of Bucharest Greece keeps Thessaloniki and southern Macedonia; with Epirus and Crete, its territory and population grow by more than half. The Ottoman garrison of Thessaloniki surrenders to the Greek army on 26 October 1912 (Old Style), a day before Bulgarian troops arrive.

BGR.art: Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, consecrated 1924, built 1882–1912. Ivan Mrkvička’s paintings of Bulgarian life. The Bulgarian national style in Sofia’s public buildings.
BGR.ideas: San Stefano Bulgaria and the claim to Macedonia. Bulgarian national unification in Macedonia. Ferdinand moves towards Germany after 1913.
BGR.literature: Ivan Vazov’s Under the Yoke; Peyo Yavorov. Yavorov’s poems; Elin Pelin’s stories. Aleko Konstantinov’s Bay Ganyo (1895).
BGR.philosophy: Liberal and agrarian politics (Stamboliyski). Agrarian and liberal politics.
BGR.story: In June 1913 Bulgaria attacks Serbia and Greece over Macedonia; Romania and the Ottomans join in, and by the Treaty of Bucharest it loses most of its gains. The Treaty of Bucharest (August 1913) leaves Bulgaria only a strip of Macedonia and Western Thrace on the Aegean; southern Dobruja goes to Romania.

ROU.art: Constantin Brâncuși in Paris. Nicolae Grigorescu’s peasant scenes; Brâncuși’s Bird in Space series begins with Măiastra (1910–12). Ștefan Luchian (d. 1916).
ROU.ideas: Union of all Romanians, including Transylvania. Union of all Romanians. The Cultural League campaigns for Transylvanian Romanians.
ROU.literature: Mihail Sadoveanu; George Enescu’s Romanian Rhapsodies (music). George Coșbuc and Octavian Goga, a Transylvanian poet. Ion Luca Caragiale (d. 1912), master of comedy; Liviu Rebreanu’s first stories.
ROU.philosophy: Titu Maiorescu’s Junimea circle. Junimea circle (Titu Maiorescu).
ROU.science: Henri Coandă; Victor Babeș. Victor Babeș’s bacteriology. Coandă’s experimental ducted aircraft shown in Paris in 1910.
ROU.story: At the Crown Council of 3 August 1914 King Carol I, a Hohenzollern, wants war beside Germany; his ministers refuse. He dies on 10 October. Romania stays neutral; Brătianu waits to see which side will give Transylvania and Bukovina.

ALB.art: Shkodër photography studio of the Marubi family. Marubi photography studio, Shkodër. Kolë Idromeno’s paintings in Shkodër.
ALB.ideas: Albanian nationalism. Albanian nationalism. The Congress of Manastir (1908) chooses the Latin alphabet.
ALB.literature: Naim Frashëri’s national poetry; the Latin-based alphabet adopted at Manastir (1908). Faik Konica’s journal Albania (Brussels, from 1897). Ndre Mjeda and Gjergj Fishta, Catholic poets of Shkodër.
ALB.philosophy: Sami Frashëri’s programme for an Albanian state.
ALB.science: The first Albanian schools and the standard alphabet of 1908. The first Albanian schools; the 1908 alphabet.
ALB.story: Wilhelm of Wied lands at Durrës in March 1914; facing a peasant revolt and the outbreak of war, he leaves in September. Qemali raises the flag of Skanderbeg at Vlorë on 28 November 1912 and proclaims independence.

TUR.art: First National Architectural style (Vedat Tek, Mimar Kemaleddin). Vedat Tek’s Central Post Office in Istanbul. Osman Hamdi Bey (d. 1910), painter and founder of the Istanbul Archaeology Museum.
TUR.ideas: Turkism, Ottomanism and Islamism competing. The Committee of Union and Progress’s Turkish nationalism. The Ottomans abolish the capitulations, foreigners’ legal privileges, in September 1914.
TUR.literature: Ömer Seyfettin’s short stories; the ‘National Literature’ movement. Halide Edib’s novels. Mehmet Akif’s Islamist poetry (Safahat).
TUR.philosophy: Ziya Gökalp’s Turkish nationalism. Gökalp’s Turkism.
TUR.science: Istanbul University (Darülfünun); German-built Baghdad railway. The Darülfünun (Istanbul University).
TUR.story: On 29 October 1914 the Ottoman fleet, led by the German battlecruiser Goeben, shells Russia’s Black Sea ports, bringing the empire into the war. Germany’s Goeben and Breslau reach Istanbul on 10 August 1914 and are ‘sold’ to the Ottoman navy, keeping their German crews.

MNE.art: Cetinje’s royal palace and legations. Cetinje’s royal palace and legations. Cetinje’s court and government buildings.
MNE.ideas: Union with Serbia versus the Petrović dynasty. Union with Serbia versus the Petrović dynasty. Nicholas I’s autocracy versus the Club party. The Podgorica-centred opposition favours union with Serbia.

images.alt: Siege of Scutari, 1913: Ottoman defenders with a captured Montenegrin standard
images.caption: Siege of Scutari, 1913: Ottoman defenders with a captured Montenegrin standard

MNE.literature: Petar II Petrović-Njegoš’s The Mountain Wreath (1847). Njegoš. King Nicholas himself writes poetry and plays, including The Empress of the Balkans (1884).
MNE.philosophy: Njegoš. Njegoš. Njegoš’s The Mountain Wreath as a national epic.
MNE.science: Cetinje’s gymnasium and printing press. Cetinje’s gymnasium and printing press. The Cetinje printing press, successor of the fifteenth-century Crnojević press.
MNE.story: In 1913 Montenegro captures Scutari (Shkodër) after a long siege, then has to hand it over to the new Albania under great-power pressure. King Nicholas has ruled since 1860; his court is famous for marrying daughters into European royalty, including Elena, Queen of Italy.
